1:
Delitzsch opens by describing the position Hezekiah inherited and the programme he set himself. The pious son of a godless father recognised that the business of his reign was to bring the kingdom out of the ruin into which Ahaz had led it by idolatry and by a heathen foreign policy, and to raise it again in religion, in morals and in political standing. Two undertakings followed from that: first the abolishing of idolatry and the restoring of the worship according to the law, and afterwards the throwing off of subjection to Assyria.

What Delitzsch does with that observation is turn it into a point about the two histories. Both books tell the same reign, but they weight it differently. The older account gives the removal of idolatry and the king's faithfulness very briefly, and spends its length on the revolt against Assyria — Sennacherib's invasion, the destruction of his army before the city, and everything that followed from it. This book reverses the proportions, and the chapter at hand is the reason: the cleansing of the temple gets the space that the other account gives to the war.

On the notice that the king did what was right, the witnesses are brief because the verse is. Ellicott observes that it stands identical with its counterpart in the older book, word for word. Clarke simply refers his reader to his own note there rather than repeating himself.

The date, however, Delitzsch finds genuinely disputed. The text puts the opening of the doors in the first month of the first year of the reign, and he sets out why interpreters differ: the Levites began the purification on the first day of that month, reached the porch within eight days and finished on the sixteenth, while the king's summons to the priests and Levites had come before any of that. He lets the difficulty stand rather than resolving it by adjusting one of the figures. He adds one detail from the parallel that this chapter omits — that the doors Hezekiah repaired were overlaid with leaf-gold. Delitzsch's larger point about the two undertakings bears on the date as well: if the religious reform came first and the revolt from Assyria afterwards, then a purification begun in the opening month of the reign is exactly what his reconstruction requires, and the chapter's chronology and its theology are making the same claim.
3:
Which first month is meant matters, and Ellicott answers it flatly: Nisan, the first month of the sacred year, not the first month of the reign. Gill adds the day from the later verse, the first of that month. The doors the king opened are the ones his father had shut, and Ellicott takes the repairing to mean overlaying them with metal, bronze or gold-leaf — so the first act of the reign is to undo the last act of the previous one, in the same material.

The summons follows, and Delitzsch is careful about where it was issued. The priests and Levites were gathered into the open space on the east, in front of the temple, rather than into the inner court as some have supposed. Gill identifies them simply as the men who officiated in the temple service, and Ellicott renders the verb as caused to come.

What they were told to do has an order to it that Delitzsch will not let collapse. They were to sanctify themselves first and the house afterwards, because the work of purifying the sanctuary had to be undertaken in a state of Levitical purity — a man cannot cleanse what he is himself unfit to approach. Gill describes the self-sanctifying concretely: washing their bodies and their garments, so that no pollution should attend them in their service.

The uncleanness to be carried out is named with a word Delitzsch traces through the chapter. Here it is the term for Levitical impurity, exchanged later for another; and what it refers to in this instance is the abominations of idolatry rather than any ordinary defilement. He notes that the king grounds the whole summons in two things — the devastation Ahaz and his generation had worked in the house of God, and the wrath that had come upon the nation on account of it. The cleansing is presented as a response to a judgement already fallen, not as a precaution against one.

Gill's reading of the self-sanctifying is worth setting beside Delitzsch's. Where Delitzsch states the principle — that purity must run from the men to the building and not the other way — Gill describes the act, and between them the verse gets both its logic and its practice. Neither treats the washing as symbolic merely; it is the condition on which the rest of the chapter can proceed at all.
6:
The king's indictment of the previous generation is blunt, and the witnesses notice that it is also careful. Gill identifies the fathers as the immediate ancestors — his own father and theirs — and calls their idolatry a great trespass, than which there is no greater evil in God's sight nor anything more provoking. Ellicott sharpens the verb to dealt unfaithfully, and works on the two phrases about turning. Turning the face away from the habitation and turning the back are set side by side; the second is literally to give the neck, a phrase that ordinarily means to be put to flight, used here in the sense of the commoner expression for turning the neck away. From the following verse, Ellicott says, it is clear the description is meant of Ahaz and his own generation.

Wesley catches what the king does not say. He says they, not my father — because it became him as a son to be as tender as he could of his father's name. The charge is unsparing about the deeds and silent about the man, and Wesley treats that silence as filial rather than evasive.

What was shut down is itemised, and Ellicott takes each item in turn. The porch is the porch of the holy place, the only way into the two inner chambers, so closing it stopped everything; Gill says the same more shortly, that there was no entering the temple. The lamps put out were those of the great golden stand; the incense not burned was the incense of the golden altar. On the word sanctuary Ellicott is precise: it does not mean the holy place alone but the whole sacred precinct, courts and buildings together. And he explains why the text can say no burnt offering was presented when Ahaz had in fact kept an altar going — the offerings made on the new Syrian altar are counted as nothing, being irregular.

Then the consequence, which the king points at rather than argues. Gill lists what the wrath looked like in practice: the Syrians, the Israelites, the Edomites and the Philistines allowed to come up and distress them. Delitzsch reads the clause as ye see with your eyes as pointing to exactly those defeats under Ahaz, together with the oppression by the Syrian king. Neither treats the appeal as rhetorical; the audience had lived through the evidence.
9:
The losses are named before the remedy is proposed. Gill identifies the fathers fallen by the sword as those killed in great numbers by the kings of Syria and Israel, and the captivity as the fate of the wives and children left behind. The verse gives the king's motive in the plainest possible terms: this is what the anger has already cost.

Against that, the proposal. Delitzsch explains what making a covenant means here — not a new arrangement but the renewal of the existing one, accomplished by restoring the worship that had lapsed; and he notes that this is why the summons to the Levites follows immediately, since the restoring is their work to do. Gill reads it the same way and supplies the precedent, that Asa and Jehoiada had each renewed the covenant before. Clarke goes further back, to the covenant under which the whole people were constantly held and of which circumcision was the sign, whose spirit he states in seven words: I will be your God, ye shall be my people.

Ellicott stays with the grammar. The preposition governing the covenant is for rather than with, and the verb translated turn away is literally return — the anger is asked to go back rather than merely to cease.

The address to the Levites is where the chapter's tone changes, and both Gill and Delitzsch stop on the word the king uses. My sons: Gill hears in it a father speaking to his people in the most tender and affectionate manner, and Delitzsch calls it kindly language deliberately chosen. The charge itself is not to be negligent, and Delitzsch notes that the verb in this form occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew, carrying the sense of letting a thing slip through carelessness rather than refusing it outright. That is the failure the king is guarding against — not rebellion but drift.

Ellicott's observation about the verb is worth holding alongside that. The anger is asked to return, to go back where it came from, rather than simply to stop; and the covenant is made for the Lord rather than with him. Both are small adjustments of preposition and voice, and both push the sentence away from negotiation and toward petition.

Delitzsch adds what happened next, and it is the answer to the whole speech: the address was heard with gladness. The Levites gathered their brethren, sanctified themselves, and set to work.
12:
Fourteen men are named, and both Gill and Ellicott find a pattern in the number. Gill walks the list: two of the Kohathites, two of the Merarites, two of the Gershonites, two of the house of Elizaphan, and then two from each of the three musical families founded under David — Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, whom he identifies with Ethan. Ellicott describes the same arrangement as seven pairs, two from each of the three great Levitical houses and two from each of the remaining musical guilds, making fourteen principal men of the order. The delegation is representative rather than assembled at random.

What those fourteen did next depended on their standing. Ellicott points out that as heads of houses they had the authority to summon their brethren, and that the families most concerned would naturally be those living in the capital. Delitzsch says the same and adds the sequence: they gathered the other Levites of Jerusalem, then all of them sanctified themselves, and only then went forward with the cleansing.

The phrase describing their warrant is read alike by both. Delitzsch attaches the words about the words of the Lord to the king's commandment rather than to the cleansing, and Ellicott spells out what that yields — a mandate of the king's that was itself grounded in what stood written in the law. The Levites are not obeying a royal whim, and the text is at pains to say so.

Wesley alone asks what cleansing a long-shut building actually involved, and his answer is domestic before it is theological. There was the dirt the house had contracted while it stood closed: dust, cobwebs, the rust on the vessels. And then, far more, the idols and the idolatrous altars. Putting the two in that order is the point — the work began as sweeping and ended as reformation, and the same men did both.

Delitzsch adds the detail that makes the sequence intelligible: the fourteen did not act alone but assembled the wider body of Levites resident in the city, so that a delegation of heads became a working party. The chapter has moved in four verses from a king's speech to men with brooms, and the witnesses follow it down without treating the descent as a fall.
16:
The cleansing was divided by who was allowed where, and Clarke lays the division out most clearly. The courts, both of the priests and of the people, were done first and took eight days. Then the interior; and because the Levites had no right to enter the building, the priests carried the dirt and rubbish out as far as the porch, where the Levites collected it, took it away, and cast it into the brook Kidron. That accounted for eight days more, and sixteen in all. Delitzsch describes the same relay from the text — priests bringing the uncleanness out into the court, Levites carrying it beyond the city — and gives the timetable in the same shape: the courts from the first day, the porch reached on the eighth, the whole finished on the sixteenth.

How far into the building the priests went is a question Gill raises on his own. The inner part he takes for the holy place, where the lampstands and the tables stood and which none but priests might enter. The most holy place was another matter, barred to everyone but the high priest and to him only on the day of atonement — though Gill allows that in case of necessity, as for repairs, others might go in, and supposes they may have done so here if any pollution had reached it. He does not claim more than that.

On the date Gill weighs two readings, the first month of the reign or the first of the year, and prefers the year, naming the month from the Targum.

The report to the king closes the section, and the vessels in it produce the chapter's sharpest small disagreement. The text says Ahaz cast them away. Gill will not take that literally: the vessels were gold and silver and too valuable to discard, so following Kimchi he reads it as removing them and turning them to idolatrous use, or with the Targum as defiling and profaning them. Ellicott keeps the harder sense, matching the verb to the word used elsewhere for casting off, and names the pieces — the brazen altar, the brazen sea, the lavers on their stands. Delitzsch splits the difference with a gloss: thrown away, that is, made worthy of rejection. Clarke reports a Targum that goes further than any of them, saying the polluted vessels were collected and hidden and that others were prepared to replace them.

Ellicott adds one word to the report's own vocabulary. What the Levites say they have done to the vessels is not merely gathering but ordering aright, putting them to rights — and the form of the verb, he notes, occurs only here.
20:
The king moved the moment the house was ready. Gill reads his rising early as taking the first opportunity to attend the worship of God and setting an example to his people; Henry says he lost no time. Ellicott explains why only the rulers of the city were summoned rather than the nation: there was no time to send a general call into the country, because Hezekiah meant to proceed at once with the sacrifices of expiation.

Henry states what those sacrifices were for, and will not let the reformation stand in their place. Atonement had to be made for the sins of the last reign, and it was not enough to lament those sins and forsake them — a sin offering was brought. He draws the conclusion forward: repentance and reformation do not themselves obtain pardon, which comes only in and through Christ.

The scale of the offering interests Gill, because the law required one goat and here there are seven of each kind. He accounts for it two ways: the multitude of transgressions committed, and the length of time during which sacrifice had been neglected altogether. He also distributes the purpose as the verse does — for the king with his family and court, among whom idolatry had prevailed in his father's day; for the sanctuary that Ahaz had polluted; and for the expiation of the whole land.

Ellicott follows the ritual itself with unusual attention, and explains why it is described at such length. The blood was caught in bowls and thrown toward the altar; the verb for killing is the one reserved for sacrificial slaughter; and the three clauses of the verse are built symmetrically. That repetition, he says, is a mark of the writer's anxiety to show how carefully the legitimate ritual was observed at every step — after a reign in which the altar itself had been irregular, the exactness is the point.

The laying on of hands draws out the meaning of the whole. Clarke takes the gesture as confession: the offerers had by their transgression forfeited their own lives, and they now present these animals to die in their place, a life taken for a life. Ellicott describes what the priests then did with the blood — a finger dipped, the horns of the altar touched, the rest poured out at its base — and reads the closing clause as extending the offering's scope, since the king had commanded burnt offering and sin offering for all Israel, an expression that takes in the northern kingdom as well.
25:
With the sacrifice ordered, the music is restored, and Gill notes what that restoration implies: cymbals, psalteries and harps were the three principal instruments of worship, and all three had fallen into disuse under Ahaz. Delitzsch identifies them simply as the instruments whose use David had introduced into the public service, and Gill says the same of the phrase about David's instruments — invented, directed and ordered by him.

Clarke stops here longer than anyone, because he thinks the verse raises a question the others pass over. Moses appointed no musical instruments for divine worship at all; there was nothing of the kind under the first tabernacle, and the horns used then were not for song or praise but served the function bells serve for us, giving the congregation notice of what it was called to do. The instruments are David's innovation, and Clarke does not pretend the innovation went unchallenged: he recalls that the prophet Amos reproved those who devised instruments of music after the manner of David. And then he registers, without resolving it, what this chapter says instead — that the arrangement came by commandment.

That tension is left standing rather than argued away, and it is the most interesting thing in the passage. The text before him asserts divine authority for the music; the prophet he cites treats such music as a mark of complacency; Clarke reports both and leaves the reader holding them. It is a rare thing in this apparatus for a commentator to quote a prophet against the practice his own text is commending, and rarer still to do it without immediately explaining the difficulty away.

The timing of the two acts is what Delitzsch attends to. The clause about commanding the burnt offering is repeated from earlier in the chapter, he observes, simply to make a connection for what follows — and what follows is a synchronism. At the moment the sacrificial act began, the song of the Lord began too, with the trumpets and with David's instruments together. Gill describes the offering itself as wholly devoted to God, an acknowledgement of his sovereignty and of his goodness, which is why the praise and the burning start at the same instant rather than one after the other.
28:
The description of the service itself is where Ellicott finds the passage most valuable, and he says so: these verses throw a particular light on how the worship was actually conducted. He renders the verbs as continuous — the congregation were worshipping, the clarions were blowing — and points out an idiom the English flattens. The Hebrew says not the singers but the song, as we might say that the music was playing; and where it names the clarions the participle is masculine though the noun is feminine, because the instrument stands for the men playing it, exactly as an orchestra is said to have violins when it means violinists.

Gill describes the congregation's part in a phrase: they bowed their heads as a token of divine adoration. What the text is careful to say, and Ellicott keeps, is that the whole of it continued until the burnt offering was finished — the music was not an accompaniment that stopped when attention wandered but something coextensive with the sacrifice.

When the offering ended the posture changed. Delitzsch notes that the king and everyone present knelt and worshipped at the close of the sacrificial act, and Gill specifies that both the sin offering and the burnt offering were meant. Then a second command followed, this time from the king and the princes together: the Levites were to sing praise in the words of David and of Asaph. Gill observes that these were psalms composed by the one and the other, and passes on Jarchi's identification of the particular psalm used. Delitzsch adds how it was received — they sang with joy, and bowed themselves.

The section closes with Hezekiah speaking again, and Delitzsch explains the idiom the king uses. To have filled the hand to the Lord is to have been consecrated to his service; the king is telling the priests and Levites that they now stand consecrated afresh, and on that ground inviting the congregation to come near with their sacrifices and thank offerings. The invitation rests on the cleansing just completed rather than on the willingness of those who receive it, which is why the king can issue it as a consequence rather than as a request.
32:
The totals are given, and Gill sorts them by who ate what. The burnt offerings — seventy bullocks, a hundred rams, two hundred lambs — left the offerers no portion at all, being wholly devoted to God in thankfulness. The consecrated things, six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep, were peace offerings, of which the owners did have a share. Delitzsch gives the same figures and calls the spontaneous contribution very large.

Gill then does something the others do not, and sets the numbers in proportion. They are much smaller than what was offered in the days of David and Solomon, and he gives two reasons: the nation was poorer than it had been, and this was the oblation of two tribes rather than of all Israel. The generosity is real and the diminishment is real, and he records both.

The shortage of priests is the chapter's most pointed detail, and the witnesses handle it carefully. Gill explains the practical problem — flaying the burnt offerings was priests' work and there were not enough of them to do it. Ellicott adds a second reason the Levites were needed: the priests who were available were fully occupied with the service of the altar itself. Gill enlarges on how much there was to do, since every burnt offering carried its meat and drink offering, and the fat of the peace offerings had to be burnt besides.

But the text supplies a reason of its own, and Delitzsch reports it without softening: the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests were. The bottleneck was not merely numerical. Enough priests existed; not enough had made themselves ready, and the men of the lower order had been readier than the men of the higher. The chapter states this in passing, as an explanation of a staffing difficulty, and leaves it there.

The closing verse turns on how one clause is read. Delitzsch takes the rejoicing to be over what God had prepared for the people — meaning the purified house and the restored worship — and explicitly rejects the alternative construction, which would make it joy that God had made the people themselves ready. Gill reads the gladness more simply, as delight at seeing things go so well, which boded good for what was coming. On the last clause all agree, and Delitzsch notes that it is what heightened the joy: the whole thing had been done suddenly. Clarke ends where the chapter does, with king and people rejoicing together at what God had brought about.
